# Bivariate Benefit-Risk Synthesis of DOACs versus Warfarin in Atrial Fibrillation

---

## Abstract

**Background:** Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are compared with warfarin for
stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation (AF) on two axes simultaneously —
efficacy (stroke/systemic embolism) and safety (major bleeding). A bivariate
synthesis makes the trade-off explicit.

**Methods:** We meta-analysed high-dose DOAC vs warfarin in the four pivotal
trials — RE-LY [1], ROCKET-AF [2], ARISTOTLE [3], ENGAGE-AF [4] — for stroke/
systemic embolism and major bleeding. Log-effects were pooled by REML random
effects with a Hartung-Knapp 95% CI (t_{k-1}, q≥1 floor); we report Cochran Q,
I², and prediction intervals, and computed illustrative absolute effects.

**Results:** DOACs reduced **stroke/systemic embolism** (pooled RR **0.81**,
HKSJ 95% CI 0.66–0.98; I²=41%; normal-approx CI 0.72–0.91) — matching the
published benchmark (0.81, 0.73–0.91) [5]. **Major bleeding** was similar on
average (pooled RR **0.85**, 0.64–1.13) but **highly heterogeneous (I²=83%,
Q=18.2)**, ranging from 0.69 (apixaban) to 1.04 (rivaroxaban). Thus efficacy is a
consistent class effect while bleeding risk is agent-specific. Illustrative
absolute effects (warfarin baseline rates): ~3.0 fewer stroke/SE, ~3.6 fewer
intracranial haemorrhages, and ~4.1 fewer deaths per 1000 patient-years [5].

**Conclusion:** As a class, DOACs offer a consistent stroke-prevention benefit
over warfarin with lower intracranial haemorrhage and mortality, but the
bleeding trade-off is not a class property — it is agent-dependent (I²=83%),
which is precisely what a bivariate synthesis reveals and a single pooled
bleeding number conceals.

---

## 1. Introduction

DOACs (dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban) replaced warfarin as
first-line anticoagulation in AF on the strength of four large non-inferiority/
superiority trials [1–4]. Because anticoagulation is intrinsically a benefit-risk
decision — preventing thromboembolism at the cost of bleeding — the clinically
relevant question is not efficacy alone but the joint efficacy-safety profile,
and whether that profile is a property of the class or of individual agents. We
address this with an explicit bivariate meta-analysis.

---

## 2. Methods

High-dose DOAC-vs-warfarin estimates for stroke/systemic embolism (ITT/as-
randomised) and major bleeding were extracted and **verified against each trial's
primary publication**. Log-effect variances were derived from the reported 95%
CIs. Each endpoint was pooled separately by REML random effects with a
Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman 95% CI (t_{k−1}, q≥1 floor); Cochran Q, I², and 95%
prediction intervals are reported. Illustrative absolute effects were computed
from the pooled/benchmark RRs applied to warfarin-arm baseline event rates
(stated as assumptions). Estimates were cross-validated against the four-trial
meta-analysis of Ruff et al. [5].

---

## 3. Results

### 3.1 Efficacy — stroke or systemic embolism

| Trial (agent) | RR/HR (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| RE-LY (dabigatran 150) | 0.66 (0.53–0.82) |
| ROCKET-AF (rivaroxaban, ITT) | 0.88 (0.74–1.03) |
| ARISTOTLE (apixaban) | 0.79 (0.66–0.95) |
| ENGAGE-AF (edoxaban HD, ITT) | 0.87 (0.73–1.04) |
| **Pooled (REML, HKSJ)** | **0.81 (0.66–0.98)**; I²=41%, Q=5.05 |
| Benchmark Ruff 2014 [5] | 0.81 (0.73–0.91) |

The pooled efficacy estimate (0.81) reproduces the published benchmark exactly.
Moderate heterogeneity (I²=41%) reflects the larger dabigatran-150 effect (0.66),
but the prediction interval and normal-approx CI (0.72–0.91) keep the class
benefit clearly on the side of DOACs.

### 3.2 Safety — major bleeding

| Trial (agent) | HR (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| RE-LY (dabigatran 150) | 0.93 (0.81–1.07) |
| ROCKET-AF (rivaroxaban) | 1.04 (0.90–1.20) |
| ARISTOTLE (apixaban) | 0.69 (0.60–0.80) |
| ENGAGE-AF (edoxaban HD) | 0.80 (0.71–0.91) |
| **Pooled (REML, HKSJ)** | **0.85 (0.64–1.13)**; **I²=83%, Q=18.2** |
| Benchmark Ruff 2014 [5] | 0.86 (0.73–1.00) |

The pooled bleeding estimate (0.85) matches the benchmark, but the **I²=83%** is
the key finding: major-bleeding risk is highly heterogeneous across DOACs,
spanning a clinically important reduction (apixaban 0.69) to no difference
(rivaroxaban 1.04). A single pooled bleeding RR is therefore a misleading summary
— bleeding safety is an agent-level, not class-level, property.

### 3.3 Bivariate profile and illustrative absolute effects

Placing the two axes together: efficacy is a **consistent** class benefit
(I²=41%, all four trials favour DOACs or are neutral), whereas bleeding is
**heterogeneous** (I²=83%). Using warfarin-arm baseline rates, the class-level
absolute effects per 1000 patient-years are approximately (benchmark RRs [5]):

| Outcome | Baseline (warfarin) | RR | Absolute effect / 1000py |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stroke/SE | 1.6%/yr | 0.81 | ~3.0 fewer (NNT ≈ 330) |
| Intracranial haemorrhage | 0.7%/yr | 0.48 | ~3.6 fewer (NNT ≈ 275) |
| All-cause mortality | 4.1%/yr | 0.90 | ~4.1 fewer (NNT ≈ 245) |
| GI bleeding | — | 1.25 [5] | increased (agent-dependent) |

(Baselines are trial-derived assumptions, stated as such; ICH/mortality/GI RRs
are the verified Ruff pooled values [5].)

---

## 4. Discussion

The bivariate view yields a message neither axis gives alone. **Efficacy** is a
robust class effect: all four agents reduce or match warfarin for stroke/SE, the
pooled 0.81 is reproducible, and the reduction in the most feared bleeding
complication (intracranial haemorrhage, RR ~0.48) and in mortality (~0.90) makes
the net direction clearly favourable. **Safety on major bleeding**, however, is
not a class property — I²=83% means the choice of agent materially changes the
bleeding trade-off, with apixaban and edoxaban more favourable and rivaroxaban
neutral. Clinically, this supports individualising DOAC selection by bleeding
risk rather than treating "DOACs" as interchangeable on safety.

Methodologically, the paper illustrates why heterogeneity statistics belong in
every benefit-risk synthesis: the efficacy pool (I²=41%) justifies a single
class summary, whereas the bleeding pool (I²=83%) does not — a pooled bleeding RR
of 0.85 with a prediction interval spanning 0.48–1.54 would mislead if reported
without its heterogeneity. That our pooled estimates match Ruff 2014 [5] on both
axes confirms the reproduction while the explicit I² adds the interpretive layer.

---

## 5. Limitations

Trial-level (aggregate) synthesis of high-dose regimens; endpoint and
bleeding-definition harmonisation differs across trials (ISTH vs trial-specific),
contributing to the bleeding heterogeneity. Only four trials (k=4), limiting
heterogeneity-estimate precision. Absolute effects use assumed warfarin baseline
rates and are illustrative, not trial-pooled. Low-dose regimens (different
profile [5]) are not analysed. Head-to-head DOAC comparisons are absent; agent
ranking on bleeding is indirect.

---

## 6. Conclusion

Across the four pivotal AF trials, DOACs reduce stroke/systemic embolism as a
consistent class effect (pooled RR 0.81, I²=41%), matching the published
benchmark, with fewer intracranial haemorrhages and lower mortality. Major
bleeding is similar on average (0.85) but **highly heterogeneous (I²=83%)** —
agent-specific, not a class property. A rigorous benefit-risk synthesis must
report both axes with their heterogeneity: the efficacy benefit generalises; the
bleeding trade-off must be individualised by agent.
